slides.text:
A slice has a length, the values it shows, and a **capacity**, the room it has to grow before it needs a bigger place. Knowing both explains why slices sometimes share values and sometimes do not.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
slice shows 2 values
room for 5 values in total
length = 2, capacity = 5

slides.text:
Three sessions:

- **1:** reading the capacity
- **2:** append with and without room
- **3:** the room left behind a cut

Behind a slice there is a stretch of values. The length is how many the slice shows, and the capacity is how many it could show, counting from where it starts to the end of that stretch.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
values = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
slice starts at 3, shows 3, 4
length = 2
capacity = 3 (3, 4, 5)

slides.text: `len` gives the length and `cap` gives the capacity. A slice can be cut again up to its capacity, even past its length.

exercises.title: Length and capacity
exercises.guide: Read both numbers of a slice with `len` and `cap`.

chunks.guide: `make` takes a third number: the capacity. This slice shows 2 values and has room for 5.

notes.text: How many items fit before append must grow.

chunks.guide: A literal has exactly as much room as values.
Without a third number, `make` gives the capacity the same value as the length.

exercises.title: A cut changes the room
exercises.guide: Cut a slice and see how much room the piece has.

chunks.guide: A slice of five values, and a piece that starts at index 1.
The piece shows 2 values, but its room runs from index 1 to the end of `s`: 4 values.

notes.text: Counts from where t starts, not from 0.

chunks.guide: A slice can be cut up to its capacity, so `t` can reach values past its own length.

notes.text: Stretches t over the spare room, up to cap.

exercises.title: Fill the buffer
exercises.guide: Add a value to `buf` and store it, then print its length and its capacity.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    buf := make([]int, 0, 4)
    buf = ___(buf, 1)
    fmt.Println(len(buf), ___(buf))
}

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `t` starts at index 2 of `s`, so its room is 3 values, and cutting it up to 3 reaches the last value of `s`.

slides.text:
When there is room, `append` writes the new value into the stretch the slice already looks at. Another slice over the same stretch sees it.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
values = 0, 0, _, _
list shows 0, 0
append 9 to list
values = 0, 0, 9, _

slides.text: When the room is full, `append` makes a new, bigger stretch and copies the values into it. The result no longer shares anything with the old slice. How much bigger the new stretch is depends on Go, so a program should not count on it.

exercises.title: Append with room to spare
exercises.guide: Append to a slice that has room and see who notices.

chunks.guide: A slice of 2 values with room for 4, and an append that fits in that room.
`t` and `s` look at the same values, so a change through `t` shows in `s`.

notes.text: No copy was made, so s sees it too.

chunks.guide: `s` keeps its length. The capacity did not change either, because nothing new was made.
The value `append` wrote is still there, just past the length of `s`.

notes.text: Reaches past len into the spare room.

exercises.title: Append with no room
exercises.guide: Append to a slice that is full and see what separates.

chunks.guide: A slice with no room left, so the append has to make a new stretch of values.
`t` has its own values now. Changing it does not reach `s`.
And changing `s` does not reach `t`.

exercises.title: Limit the room
exercises.guide: Cut a piece that cannot write into the original.

chunks.guide: A third number in the cut sets where the room ends. `s[:2:2]` shows 2 values and has room for 2.

notes.text: The last number caps the room.

chunks.guide: The piece has no spare room.
With no room, the append makes new values, and `s` stays as it was.

exercises.title: A safe piece
exercises.guide: Take the first three values of `s`, with the room limited so that the append can never change `s`.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    a := make([]int, 1, 3)
    b := append(a, 5)
    c := append(a, 6)
    fmt.Println(b[1], c[1], len(a))
}
exercises.explanation: Both appends fit in the room of `a`, so both write to index 1 of the same values. The second write wins, and `a` keeps its length of 1.

slides.text:
A piece cut from the start or the middle of a slice has the values after it as spare room. They are not shown, but they are still there, and `append` writes over them.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
values = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
head shows 1, 2 (room for 5)
append 99 to head
values = 1, 2, 99, 4, 5

slides.text:
This is why removing a value with `append(s[:i], s[i+1:]...)` also moves the values of the original slice. The result fits in the room that was already there.

To stop a piece from writing into the original, limit its room with a third number in the cut.

exercises.title: Append after a cut
exercises.guide: Append to a piece and look at the original.

chunks.guide: A slice of five values, and a piece with the first two.
The piece shows 2 values, but its room reaches the end of `s`.
The append fits in that room, so it writes over the third value of `s`.

exercises.title: The room a remove uses
exercises.guide: Remove a value and see what the original keeps.

chunks.guide: Keep a second name for the same values, then remove index 1.
The result has 4 values, and the room of 5 did not change.
The values moved left inside the same stretch. The last place still holds its old value.

exercises.title: A head that cannot write
exercises.guide: Take the first two values of `s` and add 9, without ever changing `s`. Then print the length of the head.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `b` has room for 3 values, so the append writes into `a` and nothing is copied. The capacity stays 3.

exercises.title: Limit a piece in the middle
exercises.guide: Cut a piece from the middle and cap its room.

chunks.guide: The third number is the end of the room, counted like the second one. `s[1:3:4]` shows 2 values and has room for 3.
This append fits the room, so it reaches `s`.
The room is now full, so this append makes new values. Changing `mid` no longer reaches `s`.
